Bei der privaten Evaluierung werden verschieden-aussehende Seiten genutzt. D. h., dass unser Agent, ob Clef, Qwen, oder ein Pattern Matching System um die Seite richtig zu verstehen. Die Seiten sind auch sehr trickhaft ausgelegt. Z. B. gibt es Zeitzonen und auf dem ERP auch Bilder mit Text sowie ab und zu Aufforderungen, das Portal zu bewerten. Also das mit Playwright muss ordentlich funktionieren um nicht ausgetrickst zu werden. Schreibe eine Agents.md Datei und weitere Dokummentation die wir in die Prompts synchronisieren können, um dann unsere Aufgaben einzuteilen. Es muss alles richtig klappen, deswegen brauchen wir intensives Testing. Lies dir auch auf der Atira Seite durch, wie genau wir die Performance von unserem Agent evaluieren können. Google auch, bzw such dir auf Github Inspiration von anderen Projekten durch, wie wir optimal hervorgehen können, damit wir von anderen Fehlern im voraus lernen. Sammel deshalb im voraus schon common Fehler und klau gute Features, damit wir die höchsten Gewinnchancen haben. Wir müssen schnell iterieren und etwas wie ein MVP erst einmal haben. Kannst so viel machen wie du willst. Sei kein Idiot und mache wenige Fehler. Erst einmal die Documentation, damit das Team anfangen kann zu arbeiten parallel. Die 5 Leute sind gerade alle arbeitslos. https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/ https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/announcements https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start

The challenge
From RFQ to bid
Turn a public tender into a correct, signed bid without a person touching it.
You work for a German hydraulics manufacturer that wants to bid on a public tender for hydraulic cylinders. What you need is spread over four websites: the tender portal, a supplier portal with the buyer's specification, your company's ERP and the sales inbox. They behave like real business software, with logins, popups, session timeouts and outdated documents. Your agent reads all of it, applies the bid rules and enters one priced, signed bid in the tender portal.
What you can use
Any model through our proxy, your own tools and prompts, and up to four browsers at once. A model does the work in the sandbox: it finds its way through the websites and makes the decisions during the run. No fixed scripts, no crawlers, no copied values, no person helping.
How you win
Your bid has to be eligible first. After that, the most accurate bid wins, and between equally accurate bids, the cheaper and faster one. The leaderboard uses the public data. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.

Public and private data
There are two datasets. The leaderboard uses the public one, on these websites. The final run uses a private dataset: the same jobs, bid rules and answer format, on different websites with other content and data. We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order: performance on the private dataset, performance on the public dataset, and the elegance of the system.
Public dataset
The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too.
Private dataset
When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario.
The rules
The brief states these rules in full. Together they define exactly one correct answer.
01 · Quantity
The tender quantity, overridden by the latest clarification that changes that position.
02 · Requirement
The position's requirement in the specification revision marked current.
03 · Material
The active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification match exactly. If a position has none, the answer is no bid.
04 · Unit price
The price condition valid on the scenario date, at the highest quantity scale reached, minus the approved discount, rounded half-up to the cent.
05 · Discount
The most recent approval from the sales director for this exact tender; otherwise 0 %.
06 · Lead time
The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
07 · Total
The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
08 · Decision
Bid, with one entry per tender position; no bid with no positions and a total of 0 when a material is missing.
09 · Partial submission
Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
10 · Finding records
The specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
11 · Agent requirement
A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
12 · Commercial clauses
A tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
13 · Withdrawn answers
A tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer's quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
14 · Scoped amendments
After selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
15 · Shared stock
Sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
16 · Conditional discount
The latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
17 · Units
Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
18 · Pricing breakdown
Base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
19
These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
20 · Technical derivation
For a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
21 · Authority and time
Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
22 · Currency
The valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
23 · Packaging
Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
24 · Delivery
Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.
25 · Shared setup
Q&A identifies pool members; ERP gives allocation mass (distinct from surcharge mass); the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee. Allocate by quantity × allocation mass using the cent-allocation rule in that mail. Add each allocation to that position's ordinary setup fee. Report surcharge_per_unit BEFORE discount, excluding packaging and bonus.
26 · Project bonus
The finance mail gives marginal percentage bands. Compute the eligible undiscounted EUR goods total, apply each band only to its portion, round the aggregate credit HALF_UP to cents, then allocate proportionally to eligible line goods values using largest remainders in cents (ties: ascending position identifier). Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.
27 · Final price
Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
28 · Metal indices
Select the latest exact-reference Preisindizes message from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. If the code lists validity windows, use the rate whose inclusive window contains the scenario date, not the last rate listed.
29 · Scoring in bid cases
Decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, positions 75 minus any additional checks, correct total 5, arithmetic consistency 5. When present, the withdrawn Q&A quantity and date-selected metal-index checks earn 5 points each. Within each equally weighted position: material 20%, quantity 15%, base price 15%, surcharge 10%, packaging 10%, project bonus 10%, final unit price 10%, delivery 10%. Each field is independent; optional breakdown fields can be blank. No-bid scoring is unchanged.
How a run works
Develop on your machine against the public websites with the scouting logins (
atira scout --env
), then test in the sandbox:
atira test-run
uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live, or drop the package on
your team page
. A test run lasts up to 2 hours on the public data and returns its score with the full breakdown. In the commands,
$ATIRA_TOKEN
holds your personal token (sign in with
atira login
, then
atira token
).
01
Start
The run issues a token, the task brief and fresh logins for every website.
02
Read
Your agent reads the brief, the rules and the answer format from the API.
03
Work the websites
It works through the 4 websites in a real browser and gathers the facts.
04
Submit
It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.
05
Scored
The answer is checked against the one correct answer; quality, cost and time are recorded.
Develop locally
eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites
curl "https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting"   # the same, with the brief, as JSON
# run your agent on your machine, then once in the sandbox:
atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq

In a run and on your machine
In a run,
QWEN_BASE_URL
with
QWEN_API_KEY

Cost and time count toward your rank, and a call to these models costs a fraction of a frontier call. Use them for the easy steps.
If one fails mid-run, retry the call, as with any provider. If they were down for most of a run that then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count, and a scored run starts again once by itself.
Submitting
A submission is your agent as a gzipped tarball. It is reviewed automatically, then run once in the sandbox on the public dataset, and that score ranks your team. Submit as often as you like, one at a time; your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard, and your latest one that passed review goes into the final run.
agent.json
{
"setup": ["uv", "sync"],
"run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"],
"models": ["qwen"]
}
Copy
Put
agent.json
at the root of the tarball, next to your code and its dependency file. Up to 20 MB compressed.
setup
installs dependencies with network access, within 5 minutes that don't count toward your time;
run
is timed and reaches only the platform and the websites.
"browsers": 1–4
(default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts, each on its own screen.
"models"
lists the hosted models your agent calls; the run waits only for those to warm up (for all of them when it's absent). Node 24 with pnpm and bun, Python 3.12 with uv, and Rust with cargo are installed. The
starter kit
is a minimal skeleton to start from.
Upload
tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
-H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" \
-H "content-type: application/gzip" \
"https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions"
Copy
Or drop the tarball on
your team page
. Upload it as a test run first to watch it work in the sandbox: its browser live, its logs, and a recording afterwards.
Scoring and ranking
Every submission is measured on its run in the sandbox.
Quality
0 to 100. Every field of the bid is compared with the one correct answer: tender reference, positions, materials, quantities, unit prices, lead times, discount and total, each position's base price and surcharge per piece, packaging, allocated project bonus, and whether the total adds up.
Eligibility
The right tender reference; a wrong decision loses quality points but other correct fields keep their credit. A bid that is not eligible ranks after every eligible one.
Cost
Every model call goes through the proxy and is priced per model. There is no budget: at equal quality, cost × time decides.
Time
Wall-clock time from the start of the run until the answer is accepted. It weighs as much as cost: halving either halves cost × time.
Order
Eligible first
→
Quality ↓
→
Cost × time ↑
Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality. At equal quality, the lower product of cost and time wins, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time as at least 1 s, so among free runs the faster one wins.

Fair play
Your agent has to find the answer itself.
Your system must work the answer out from the websites at run time, with a model doing the navigating and deciding. A coding agent reviews every package; hardcoded answers, fixed scripts and crawlers are rejected.

Fair play
The answer must come from the websites at run time, found by a model that does the navigating and deciding, not a fixed script or a crawler. A coding agent reviews every package. Full rules
.
Team
Up to 5 people.
How you're scored
Every scored run gets a quality and an eligibility verdict; the platform measures its cost and time.
Quality
0 to 100. Every field of the bid is compared with the one correct answer: tender reference, positions, materials, quantities, unit prices, lead times, discount and total, each position's base price and surcharge per piece, packaging, allocated project bonus, and whether the total adds up.
Eligibility
The right tender reference; a wrong decision loses quality points but other correct fields keep their credit. A bid that is not eligible ranks after every eligible one.
Order
Eligible first
→
Quality ↓
→
Cost × time ↑
Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality. At equal quality, the lower product of cost and time wins, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time as at least 1 s, so among free runs the faster one wins.
On the leaderboard's plot, each dot is a team, quality against cost or time. The dotted line is the Pareto front. The quickest and cheapest passing solution might also get a small prize ;)
Answers and scoring
has every point.
Public and private data
The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too. When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario. We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order: performance on the private dataset, performance on the public dataset, and the elegance of the system.

# Atira Challenges

> Atira Challenges is a platform for agent hackathons in industrial sales. Teams build an agent system (one agent or several) that works through realistic business software, with any model through our proxy and their own tools. Each scored submission is reviewed automatically, run in an isolated sandbox on the public dataset, and ranked on a live leaderboard: eligible answers first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time. When the hackathon ends, every team's latest submission that passed review runs once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.

The public pages are also Markdown: the home page, Getting started, each challenge, its leaderboard and each team's profile. Add `.md` to the URL (`/index.md` for the home page) or send `Accept: text/markdown`. For runs, use the API or the CLI's MCP tools. Everything works with plain HTTP, so `curl` and the API guide are enough. Send your personal token (`atira token` prints it after `atira login`; plain curl can use the device flow in the API guide) or the run token in the `x-api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer`.

If you are a team's coding agent: install the CLI (`curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.sh | sh`, on Windows `irm https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.ps1 | iex`), have a team member run `atira login`, then add the CLI as your MCP server: `claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Claude Code) or `codex mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Codex). Its tools start test runs (`test_run`), wait for them (`wait_for_run`), show why one failed (`diagnose_run`, `run_logs`, `run_screenshot`, `run_inputs`) and submit (`submit`); [Debug runs from your coding agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md) lists them all. Run the agent locally against the public websites with `atira scout --env`, and start from the starter kit below. The agent you build must let a model choose where to go, what to search for and which documents matter, at run time: fixed scripts and crawlers that collect the websites for one model call are rejected in review, and so are values copied from the websites into the code.

Rules at a glance: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md

The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too. When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario.

The [leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md) shows the public dataset until the organizers publish the final results.

## Start here

- [Getting started](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start.md): what you're building, your first run step by step with every command, the scouting logins for the websites, the rules of the game and how you're scored
- [The starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz): a minimal Python skeleton to start from (reading the run, the browsers over CDP, the hosted models; the agent is yours to build), as a gzipped tarball with `agent.json` at its root

## Challenges

- [From RFQ to bid](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq.md): Your agent reads a public tender, finds the current specification, checks prices and stock in the ERP, looks up the approved discount in the sales inbox and submits one signed bid.
- [From RFQ to bid: leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md): the ranked results of scored submissions
- [From RFQ to bid: public dataset board](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md?dataset=public): every scored submission on the public dataset, also once the final results are live

## Taking part

- [Participant guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/README.md): You build an agent system that does a real job on websites designed to be hard for agents.
- [Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md): Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and ranks everyone the same way.
- [How a run works](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md): A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge.
- [Building your agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/building-an-agent.md): Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes the decisions, at run time.

- [FAQ and event details](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/faq.md)

## API

- [OpenAPI 3.1 description](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/openapi.json): every participant endpoint, with credentials, request bodies (including the gzip upload), responses and errors
- [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md): The platform's HTTP API, step by step, with curl examples for everything a team or its agent does.

- [Home](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/index.md): live totals, the top of the leaderboard and recent activity

# The CLI

A command line for taking part: one JavaScript file for Node 24 that uses only Node's built-ins. It is made for
people and coding agents alike: every command takes `--json`, and exit codes tell outcomes apart. Everything it does
# Answers and scoring

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).

## Per run

- **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
- **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
  a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
- **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
- **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.

A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.

## Leaderboard

Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
the run's own value.

1. Eligible before ineligible.
2. Higher quality.
3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
   as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
   time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.

On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
the teams no other eligible team beats on both.

Test runs on the public scenario `public-1` show the points for each part of the answer, never the expected
values. Scored runs show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.

## Final run

When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.

## Winners

We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:

1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
3. The elegance of the system.

It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).

## RFQ scoring

The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.

| Part (a bid) | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Decision | 5 |
| Tender reference | 5 |
| Discount percent | 5 |
| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |


For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
points but leaves the other fields their credit.

Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
one position's share each.

## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three

The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.

Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.

# How a run works

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
logins.

## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox

RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.

1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
   provider takes your own key.
   Nothing done with these logins counts.
   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.

## Inside a run

1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
   returns:
   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
   provider's with your own key (below).
3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
     it again.
   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.

Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.

## LLM calls

Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.

The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:

```
$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
```

`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:

| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |

The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.

### Your key

Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.

With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
as `x-api-key`:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
```

A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:

```python
import os
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
```

```javascript
import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"

const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
```

A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.

**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
`401`.

A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
context.

### How cost is measured

Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.

The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.

### Team secrets

Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:

```sh
curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
```

Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.

## Scored run

Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
`127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:

- **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
- **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
- **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
  and the websites.
- gcc, make, git, curl and jq.

1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
   to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
   run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
   never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
   them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
   `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
   right after setup:

   ```json
   {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": []}
   ```

   Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
   `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
   whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.

   **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.
   If our models were down for most of the run (from the first failed call on, a 5xx from our model or a lost
   connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run
   then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count toward ranking or
   any limit, and a scored run starts again once by itself. A
   run that answered keeps its result.
3. **Run (timed):** your `run` command starts with this environment. The clock starts here.

117	# The CLI
118	
119	A command line for taking part: one JavaScript file for Node 24 that uses only Node's built-ins. It is made for
120	people and coding agents alike: every command takes `--json`, and exit codes tell outcomes apart. Everything it does
121	# Answers and scoring
122	
123	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
124	
125	Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
126	ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
127	websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
128	isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
129	on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).
130	
131	## Per run
132	
133	- **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
134	- **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
135	  a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
136	- **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
137	- **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.
138	
139	A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
140	is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.
141	
142	## Leaderboard
143	
144	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
145	keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
146	complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
147	the run's own value.
148	
149	1. Eligible before ineligible.
150	2. Higher quality.
151	3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
152	   as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
153	   time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
154	4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.
155	
156	On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
157	the teams no other eligible team beats on both.
158	
159	Test runs on the public scenario `public-1` show the points for each part of the answer, never the expected
160	values. Scored runs show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.
161	
162	## Final run
163	
164	When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
165	answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
166	
167	## Winners
168	
169	We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:
170	
171	1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
172	2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
173	3. The elegance of the system.
174	
175	It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
176	latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
177	publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
178	public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
179	`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).
180	
181	## RFQ scoring
182	
183	The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
184	`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
185	ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
186	project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
187	The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
188	omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.
189	
190	| Part (a bid) | Points |
191	| --- | --- |
192	| Decision | 5 |
193	| Tender reference | 5 |
194	| Discount percent | 5 |
195	| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
196	| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
197	| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
198	| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
199	| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |
200	
201	
202	For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
203	points but leaves the other fields their credit.
204	
205	Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
206	one position's share each.
207	
208	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
209	
210	The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
211	Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
212	`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
213	When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
214	Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
215	counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
216	It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
217	Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
218	Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
219	on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.
220	
221	Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
222	the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
223	rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.

229	# How a run works
230	
231	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
232	
233	A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
234	logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
235	scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
236	logins.
237	
238	## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox
239	
240	RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.
241	
242	1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
243	   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
244	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
245	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
246	   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
247	   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
248	   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
249	   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
250	   provider takes your own key.
251	   Nothing done with these logins counts.
252	   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
253	2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
254	   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
255	   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
256	   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.
257	
258	## Inside a run
259	
260	1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
261	   returns:
262	   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
263	   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
264	   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
265	     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
266	   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
267	   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
268	   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
269	     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
270	   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
271	2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
272	   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
273	   provider's with your own key (below).
274	3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
275	   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
276	   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
277	   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
278	     it again.
279	   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
280	     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.
281	
282	Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
283	(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
284	front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.
285	
286	## LLM calls
287	
288	Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
289	Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
290	own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
291	API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.
292	
293	The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:
294	
295	```
296	$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
297	```
298	
299	`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:
300	
301	| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
302	| --- | --- | --- |
303	| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
304	| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
305	| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
306	| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
307	| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
308	| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
309	| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
310	| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
311	| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
312	| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |
313	
314	The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
315	each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
316	(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.
317	
318	### Your key
319	
320	Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
321	(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
322	unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
323	not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.
324	
325	With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
326	`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
327	as `x-api-key`:
328	
329	```python
330	from openai import OpenAI
331	
332	client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
333	```
334	
335	A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
336	the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:
337	
338	```python
339	import os
340	from google import genai
341	
342	client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
343	    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
344	```
345	
346	```javascript
347	import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"
348	
349	const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
350	  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
351	```
352	
353	A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
354	organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
355	key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
356	start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.
357	
358	**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
359	`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
360	(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
361	for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
362	`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
363	`401`.
364	
365	A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
366	context.
367	
368	### How cost is measured
369	
370	Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
371	provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
372	An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
373	`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
374	that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
375	a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
376	providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
377	chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
378	an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
379	early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
380	endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
381	fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.
382	
383	The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
384	charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.
385	
386	### Team secrets
387	
388	Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
389	`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:
390	
391	```sh
392	curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
393	  --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
394	curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
395	curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
396	```
397	
398	Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
399	Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
400	cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
401	`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.
402	
403	## Scored run
404	
405	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
406	ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
407	[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
408	a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
409	`127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:
410	
411	- **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
412	- **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
413	- **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
414	  and the websites.
415	- gcc, make, git, curl and jq.
416	
417	1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
418	2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
419	   to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
420	   run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
421	   never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
422	   them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
423	   `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
424	   right after setup:
425	
426	   ```json
427	   {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": []}
428	   ```
429	
430	   Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
431	   `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
432	   whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.
433	
434	   **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.
435	   If our models were down for most of the run (from the first failed call on, a 5xx from our model or a lost
436	   connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run
437	   then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count toward ranking or
438	   any limit, and a scored run starts again once by itself. A
439	   run that answered keeps its result.
440	3. **Run (timed):** your `run` command starts with this environment. The clock starts here.
441	
442	| Variable | Value |
443	| --- | --- |
444	| `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the API; read your task at `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` |
445	| `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | the run token |
446	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with this run's logins, as JSON: the same as `access` |
447	| `LLM_PROXY_URL` | `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` |
448	| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | for each model the platform hosts (`GET /v1/models/status`; the start page names them): its base URL through the proxy, under `$LLM_PROXY_URL/<provider>`, and the run token as its key |
449	| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
450	| `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
451	| `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google`; set the Gemini SDK's HTTP base URL explicitly as above |
452	| `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL`, `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral`, `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
453	| your [team secrets](#team-secrets) | for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` with your own key |
454	| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222`, browser 1 |
455	| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: `["http://127.0.0.1:9222"]` for one browser |
456	| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started: `1` unless `agent.json` asks for more |
457	| `DISPLAY` | `:1`, browser 1's screen; browser n is on `:n` |
458	| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` (and lowercase) | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`, the only way out of the sandbox |
459	| `NO_PROXY` | `localhost,127.0.0.1` (CDP stays local) |
460	
461	The platform sets no API key variables of its own, except the run-token placeholder for a provider the
462	organizers pay for (above). `setup` runs first, with network (install your dependencies there) but without the
463	run's variables or your team secrets, and nothing it starts survives into the run. The run itself reaches only our API and the challenge's websites,
464	through that proxy; Chromium is already configured to use it. A scored run of RFQ has 20 minutes; a run that
465	ends without an answer scores 0.

467	## Browsers
468	
469	The sandbox starts one browser unless `agent.json` asks for more, up to four:
470	
471	```json
472	{"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "browsers": 3}
473	```
474	
475	`browsers` is a whole number from 1 to 4; anything else rejects the package with
476	`Invalid agent.json: browsers: must be a whole number from 1 to 4`. Browser n is its own headful Chromium with its
477	own profile, on display `:n` (1280×800) with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on port 9221 + n (9222 to 9225), behind
478	the same proxy as browser 1. All of them are ready before the clock starts. `CDP_URL` stays browser 1, `CDP_URLS` lists all of
479	them in order, and `BROWSER_COUNT` says how many there are. With three:
480	
481	| Variable | Value |
482	| --- | --- |
483	| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222` |
484	| `CDP_URLS` | `["http://127.0.0.1:9222","http://127.0.0.1:9223","http://127.0.0.1:9224"]` |
485	| `BROWSER_COUNT` | `3` |
486	
487	**At most 4 browsers run at a time:** ask for up to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts
488	inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The scored sandbox enforces it:
489	any other browser the agent starts is stopped within seconds, and the run's logs say so with
490	`[platform] stopped a browser the agent started: at most 4 run at a time; use the browsers from CDP_URLS`. Every
491	browser then is one the platform can show and record: test runs show them side by side while they run, with a
492	recording of each afterwards.
493	
494	On your own machine, developing with the scouting logins, `CDP_URLS` is not set and your agent starts its own
495	browsers.

501	# Building your agent
502	
503	Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes
504	the decisions, at run time. How is up to you: drive the browser through the DOM, through pixels, or both; use one
505	model or several, in parallel if you like; give the model tools and helpers for the browser, parsing, arithmetic and
506	checks. The model chooses where to go, what to search for and which documents matter. Rejected in review: a fixed
507	script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback, and a crawler that collects the
508	websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
509	
510	## The browser
511	
512	In the sandbox a headful Chromium runs on the desktop (`DISPLAY=:1`, 1280×800) with CDP on
513	`127.0.0.1:9222`.
514	
515	- **DOM agents:** attach with Playwright (`chromium.connect_over_cdp(CDP_URL)`) or any CDP client.
516	- **Pixel agents:** take screenshots and send mouse and keyboard input to the desktop (`xdotool` and
517	  ImageMagick's `import` are installed), for example to drive Claude's computer-use tool.
518	- **Locally:** without `CDP_URL`, launch your own Chromium. The websites are the same: `eval "$(atira scout --env)"`
519	  gives your agent the scouting logins in `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS`, the way a run gets its logins.
520	
521	### Several browsers
522	
523	To work on several websites at once, ask for up to four browsers in `agent.json`:
524	
525	```json
526	{"setup": ["npm", "ci"], "run": ["node", "agent.js"], "browsers": 2}
527	```
528	
529	Each is its own Chromium on its own screen (browser n on `DISPLAY=:n`), and `CDP_URLS` lists their CDP URLs in
530	order (`CDP_URL` stays the first). With Playwright:
531	
532	```javascript
533	import { chromium } from "playwright"
534	
535	const sites = JSON.parse(process.env.CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS)
536	const browsers = await Promise.all(JSON.parse(process.env.CDP_URLS).map((url) => chromium.connectOverCDP(url)))
537	const pages = browsers.map((browser) => browser.contexts()[0].pages()[0])
538	await Promise.all([pages[0].goto(sites[0].url), pages[1].goto(sites[1].url)])
539	```
540	
541	At most 4 browsers run at a time. Use tabs (`context.newPage()`) and browser contexts (`browser.newContext()`)
542	inside them as freely as you like, but don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included: the sandbox stops
543	them and says so in the run's logs. A test run shows its browsers side by side while it runs and keeps a recording
544	of each. Locally there is no `CDP_URLS`: on your machine your agent starts its own browsers.
545	
546	## Models
547	
548	The hosted models are free to use. Every run gets `QWEN_BASE_URL` and `QWEN_API_KEY` for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an
549	OpenAI-compatible chat model with tool calls and images; on your machine `atira scout --env` sets the same variables,
550	pointed at `atira models proxy`. You can also bring your own key for any provider through the metering proxy;
551	[how cost is measured](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#how-cost-is-measured) has the details. After quality you are ranked on cost × time, so a cheaper model or a faster run that gets the answer right moves you
552	up.
553	
554	## What makes it hard, on purpose
555	
556	The websites are designed to trip agents up: cookie walls, flaky error pages that need a retry, expiring sessions
557	that send you back to the login, documents inside iframes and ZIP files, popups that close themselves, paging and
558	"load more" buttons, look-alike records, superseded versions shown first, a timezone that is not yours. Treat
559	every page as adversarial and verify what you read.
560	
561	## Tips
562	
563	- Read the brief's rules carefully: they define the one correct answer.
564	- Keep what the model reads small: page text without duplicated labels, only the parts you need.
565	- Use prompt caching for your system prompt and tool definitions.
566	- Re-read a page after every action that changes it; pages update asynchronously.
567	- Drive four browsers in parallel, one per website (`"browsers": 4`, see [Several browsers](#several-browsers)):
568	  reading the four sites at once speeds up each run and your iteration, at the cost of more complex code.
569	- Validate your answer against `answer_schema` before sending it; a `400` costs only time.
570	- Submit before the clock runs out: a scored run has 20 minutes (`expires_at` in the run). Every part of the answer
571	  scores on its own, so have your agent submit its best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
572	  searching; a run that ends without an answer scores 0.
573	- Develop against the public websites locally (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox (`atira test-run`):
574	  a test run shows the full score breakdown, so use it to find what your agent gets wrong.
575	- Work the answer out from the websites: the final run, which weighs most for the winners, uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it.
576	
577	## Starter kit
578	
579	[`starter-kit/`](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal Python skeleton, not an agent: it reads the run and
580	submits an answer, attaches to the run's browsers over CDP with Playwright, and shows one call to each hosted model.
581	Your agent goes in `solve()` in `agent.py`; out of the box it exits without an answer. Start from it or from scratch.

587	# Fair play
588	
589	**Rules at a glance**
590	
591	You submit an agentic system: one agent or several. In the sandbox it does the whole job on its own: finds what it needs on the four websites, works out the bid and submits it. Nobody helps it during a run.

Setup may install dependencies.

Facts the task brief states for every scenario, such as the sales director's mailbox, are

622	  information and makes the decisions. Code can help it (browser control, parsing, arithmetic, checks, reading a

624	  in parallel. Rejected: a fixed script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback,
